title: Born in Zion
superscription: A Psalm of the sons of Korah. A song.

verses.text: He has founded His city on the holy mountains.
The LORD loves the gates of Zion more than all the dwellings of Jacob.
Glorious things are ascribed to you, O city of God. Selah
"I will mention Rahab and Babylon among those who know Me— along with Philistia, Tyre, and Cush— when I say, 'This one was born in Zion.'"
And it will be said of Zion: "This one and that one were born in her, and the Most High Himself will establish her."
The LORD will record in the register of the peoples: "This one was born in Zion." Selah
Singers and pipers will proclaim, "All my springs of joy are in You."

context.author: The title names the sons of Korah, a family of Levites descended from the Korah who rebelled against Moses (Numbers 16). His sons did not die with him (Numbers 26:11), and their descendants became gatekeepers and singers at the Temple (1 Chronicles 9:19; 2 Chronicles 20:19).
context.genre: Psalm: a song or prayer in Hebrew poetry
context.audience: Israel at worship, in times of national crisis
context.setting: “He has founded His city on the holy mountains. The LORD loves the gates of Zion more than all the dwellings of Jacob” (vv.1-2). “Glorious things are ascribed to you, O city of God” (v.3). Then God speaks a surprise. He will count among those who know Him Israel’s old enemies and distant peoples: Rahab (Egypt), Babylon, Philistia, Tyre and Cush (v.4). Of each one it will be said, “This one was born in Zion” (v.4). “This one and that one were born in her” (v.5), and “The LORD will record in the register of the peoples” (v.6) that they belong to Zion. The singers and pipers proclaim, “All my springs of joy are in You” (v.7).
context.custom: Rahab, the name of a sea monster, was a poetic name for Egypt (Isaiah 30:7). Cities kept registers of citizens and families (Nehemiah 7:5), and to be born in a city gave the right to belong. Cush was the land south of Egypt, in modern Sudan. The psalm is short and terse, and some lines are hard to translate.
context.timelineImmediate: Psalm 88 is the darkest psalm in the Psalter, a prayer that ends in darkness.
context.timelineBible: Paul wrote, “the Jerusalem above is free, and she is our mother” (Galatians 4:26). Hebrews tells believers they have come “to Mount Zion, to the city of the living God” (Hebrews 12:22), where the firstborn are enrolled in heaven (Hebrews 12:23). John Newton’s hymn ‘Glorious Things of Thee Are Spoken’ (1779) is based on v.3.

translation.meaning: Rahab, “arrogance” or “storm”; a sea monster and a poetic name for Egypt.
To bear, give birth; to be born.

gospelParallels.note: The Jerusalem above is our mother.
You have come to Mount Zion.

otBackground.note: Egypt My people, Assyria My handiwork.
All nations will stream to it.

overview.summary: God loves Zion, and in a startling promise He enrolls even Egypt, Babylon, Philistia, Tyre and Cush as her native-born citizens.
overview.settingLine: A city whose citizens come from every nation.

archaeology.t: The lists of returning families in Ezra 2 and Nehemiah 7 resemble ancient registers.
Remains of the island city off the Lebanese coast.

overview.discussion: God writes former enemies into Zion’s register (v.4). Whom do I find hard to imagine as a fellow citizen of God’s city?
overview.book: The book of Psalms · 150 psalms (1-125 in the app so far). Israel’s songs and prayers: praise, lament, thanks, trust and wisdom, many of them by David.
overview.author: The sons of Korah
